chunks: "I think of it as a chain from the peripheral to the CPU. First, the peripheral sets a flag when the event happens, say a timer overflow.
If that peripheral's interrupt-enable bit is set, it sends a request line to the interrupt controller.
The controller, which on a Cortex-M is the NVIC, keeps an enable bit, a pending bit and a priority for each source, and picks the highest-priority pending one that is allowed.
If its priority beats whatever the CPU is currently running, and global interrupts aren't masked, it signals the core. The core checks at the end of each instruction.
It pushes the registers it must save, the program counter, status register and a few general registers, onto the stack.
Then it looks up the handler address in the vector table, which is an array of function pointers in flash indexed by interrupt number, and loads it into the program counter.
My ISR runs, and when it finishes, a special return value in the link register tells the core to pop the saved state and resume the interrupted code.

On the software side I have to do four things: configure the peripheral and enable its interrupt, enable the line in the controller and set a priority, enable global interrupts, and write a handler with the exact name the startup code put in the vector table, and clear the flag inside it."
